title: Given the heads of two singly linked lists, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If they do not intersect, return null. The intersection is by node identity, not by value, and the lists keep their original structure.
shortTitle: Intersection of Two Linked Lists: Length Diff or Two-Pass Alignment
keyPoints: Two lists intersect when they share the same tail nodes (Y-shape), detected by node reference identity not value equality
The two-pointer switching method walks A-then-B and B-then-A so both cover the same total distance and meet at the junction
If there is no intersection, both pointers become null at the same step and the loop exits cleanly
The length-difference method aligns the two pointers by advancing the longer list's pointer by the length difference first
Both methods run in O(n + m) time and O(1) space
Comparison must be reference equality (==) because two different nodes can hold the same value

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk A-then-B and B-then-A; they meet at the intersection because both cover length A plus B.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Intersection** – two singly linked lists share a common tail, forming a Y-shape; the intersection node is the first shared node by reference identity.
- **Two-pointer switch** – pointer A walks list A then list B; pointer B walks list B then list A; both traverse exactly `lenA + lenB` nodes and meet at the intersection.
- **Length-difference** – compute both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then walk both in lockstep comparing references.
- **Termination** – if no intersection, both pointers become `null` simultaneously and the loop exits.
- **Complexity** – O(n + m) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Two customers at the National Bank of India, Rajesh and Priya, each follow their own trail of linked statement nodes. At some point both trails merge into one shared trail of joint-account statements. To find where they merge, each walks their own trail and then continues onto the other person's trail. Because both cover the same total distance, they arrive at the merge point at the same moment.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Y-Shaped Intersection

  List A: [R1] ──> [R2] ──┐
                           ├──> [JOINT1] ──> [JOINT2] ──> null
  List B: [P1] ───────────┘

  Two-Pointer Switching:
  pA: R1 → R2 → J1 → J2 → null → P1 → J1 (stop)
  pB: P1 → J1 → J2 → null → R1 → R2 → J1 (stop)
  Both arrive at J1 at the same step.
```

```text
  No Intersection:

  List A: [A1] ──> [A2] ──> null
  List B: [B1] ──> null

  pA: A1 → A2 → null → B1 → null (stop)
  pB: B1 → null → A1 → A2 → null (stop)
  Both become null at the same step → return null.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the intersection of two singly linked lists means locating the exact node where two chains merge into one shared tail. The two-pointer switching method is elegant: pointer A walks list A then continues onto list B, while pointer B walks list B then continues onto list A. Both traverse exactly the combined length of both lists, so they are perfectly aligned and meet at the junction node.

If the lists do not intersect, both pointers become null at the same step after one full switch, so the loop exits cleanly and returns null. This termination guarantee is a classic follow-up question, and being able to explain why it works shows understanding rather than memorization.

The comparison must always be reference equality (`==`), not value equality, because two unrelated nodes can coincidentally carry the same amount. Intersection is a structural property: the lists literally share the same node object in memory.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, Rajesh and Priya each have personal statement chains that merge into a shared joint-account chain, forming a Y-shape. Compliance uses the intersection finder to locate the exact junction node so it can audit the shared portion for regulatory reporting.

Remember one sentence: walk A-then-B and B-then-A; both cover the same total distance and meet at the Y-junction, or both become null if there is none.
